text: Several men named Áed appear in this fragment. One Áed was held in a beautiful but barren land. He escaped that land and went to see Saint Patrick. Patrick freed him from the lingering bonds of Fairyland. The first part of the tale fits Irish myth about a fairy lover. The Saint Patrick ending looks added after Christianity came to the land. Another Áed was a son of Lir. He numbered among the Children of Lir. His jealous stepmother turned him into a swan for nine hundred years. A further Áed ruled as king of Tara. This sixth-century king owned a magic cow he believed would guard him in battle. At wartime he stayed behind without the cow. The war took his life.

okr.objective: The fairy (Irish) fragment records three separate stories of Áed.
key_results: An Áed escaped a barren land and was freed by Saint Patrick.
Áed, son of Lir, became a swan for nine hundred years through his stepmother's magic.
Áed, king of Tara, left his magic cow at home and died in war.
The Saint Patrick ending appears to be a later Christian addition.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore
